title: Traditional knowledge not patentable
text: Section 3(p) excludes an invention which in effect is traditional knowledge or is an aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known components. A company-developed combination is not exempt merely because that exact recipe is absent from classical books; whether its substance is traditional knowledge remains a claim-specific question.
review_note: Checked against the Indian statutory text hosted by WIPO Lex, archived as corpus/primary/patents-act.pdf. This verifies the cited provisions, not an exhaustive search for later amendments or case law.

title: Mere admixture (aggregation of properties) not patentable
text: Section 3(e) excludes a substance obtained by a mere admixture resulting only in aggregation of the properties of its components, and a process for producing such a substance. A multi-herb combination must be assessed against this exclusion. Comparative evidence of an effect beyond a mere aggregation can help address the exclusion; the statute does not guarantee patentability merely because a formulation is described as synergistic.
review_note: Checked against the Indian statutory text hosted by WIPO Lex, archived as corpus/primary/patents-act.pdf. This verifies the cited provisions, not an exhaustive search for later amendments or case law.

title: Methods of treatment not patentable
text: Section 3(i) excludes any process for the medicinal, surgical, curative, prophylactic, diagnostic, therapeutic or other treatment of human beings, or any similar treatment of animals to render them free of disease or to increase their economic value. A Panchakarma or therapeutic procedure per se cannot be patented (though a novel device or composition used in it may be).
review_note: Checked against the Indian statutory text hosted by WIPO Lex, archived as corpus/primary/patents-act.pdf. This verifies the cited provisions, not an exhaustive search for later amendments or case law.

title: Plants, animals and essentially biological processes not patentable
text: Section 3(j) excludes plants and animals in whole or any part thereof other than micro-organisms, including seeds, varieties and species, and essentially biological processes for their production or propagation. Claiming an ordinary medicinal plant, plant part or variety is therefore subject to this bar. Plant-variety registration is a separate, conditional route under the PPV&FR Act; it is not automatic for every medicinal plant.
review_note: Checked against the Indian statutory text hosted by WIPO Lex, archived as corpus/primary/patents-act.pdf. This verifies the cited provisions, not an exhaustive search for later amendments or case law.

title: New form of a known substance not patentable without enhanced efficacy
text: Section 3(d) excludes a mere new form of a known substance without enhancement of its known efficacy; mere discovery of a new property or new use for a known substance; and mere use of a known process, machine or apparatus unless that known process results in a new product or employs at least one new reactant. Its explanation treats listed derivatives of known substances as the same substance unless they differ significantly in properties with regard to efficacy. Assessment of a particular extract, dose, derivative or process requires claim-specific evidence and relevant case law; absence from classical texts alone does not resolve this exclusion.
review_note: Checked against the Indian statutory text hosted by WIPO Lex, archived as corpus/primary/patents-act.pdf. This verifies the cited provisions, not an exhaustive search for later amendments or case law.

title: Request for Examination window cut from 48 to 31 months
text: The Patents (Amendment) Rules, 2024 (notified by G.S.R. 211(E) and in force from 15 March 2024) substitute, in rule 24B(1), the words 'forty-eight months' with 'thirty-one months', wherever they occur. The window to file a Request for Examination is thus reduced from 48 to 31 months from the priority/filing date (applications filed before commencement retain the old 48-month period).

title: Statement of working (Form 27) now once every three financial years
text: Under the 2024 amendment, the statement of working of a patent (Form 27) must be furnished once in respect of every period of three financial years (starting from the financial year commencing immediately after grant), within six months of the expiry of each such period. The revised Form 27 no longer requires approximate revenue/value figures but the applicant must state whether the patent is available for licensing.

title: Definition of an Ayurvedic/Siddha/Unani (ASU) drug
text: Section 3(a) defines Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drugs to include all medicines intended for internal or external use for or in the diagnosis, treatment, mitigation or prevention of disease or disorder in human beings or animals, and manufactured exclusively in accordance with the formulae described in the authoritative books of Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani Tibb systems specified in the First Schedule. This 'exclusively per First-Schedule formula' test is what marks a CLASSICAL medicine.
review_note: Checked in official CDSCO compilation amended through 31 December 2016, pp.6 and 8. Classification depends on complete ingredients, their textual references, intended use and route, not a product label or patent grant.

title: Definition of a patent or proprietary medicine (ASU)
text: Section 3(h)(i) defines patent or proprietary medicines in the ASU systems as formulations containing only ingredients mentioned in formulae in the First Schedule authoritative books, while excluding parenteral medicines and formulations themselves included in those books. An original four-plant formulation potentially fits this category only if all ingredients satisfy that textual ingredient test and it is non-parenteral. The statutory word patent does not mean an invention patent has been granted or is required.
review_note: Checked in official CDSCO compilation amended through 31 December 2016, pp.6 and 8. Classification depends on complete ingredients, their textual references, intended use and route, not a product label or patent grant.

title: Licensing of ASU drugs — classical vs patent/proprietary
text: Rule 158B distinguishes ASU classical, proprietary and medicinal-plant-extract licensing categories and their evidence requirements. In II(B), the proprietary-medicine row with textual ingredients/rationale specifies published literature of ingredients and a pilot study under the relevant ASU protocol; the Schedule E(1) ingredient row requires safety study and effectiveness evidence. Part V distinguishes aqueous, hydro-alcoholic and other extracts, with different safety/effectiveness requirements. Novel extraction technique, indications and Schedule E(1) status must therefore be mapped to the correct row rather than assuming one universal clinical-trial requirement.
review_note: Checked official2016 compilation pp182-184 and supplied2024 CDSCO compilation pp178-181. The supplied2024 document itself directs Ayush rule discrepancies to the Ministry of Ayush. Current application-specific studies must be confirmed with the licensing authority.

title: Good Manufacturing Practices for ASU drugs
text: Schedule T prescribes the Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) for Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani drug manufacturing units — covering factory premises, hygiene, machinery, quality control and documentation. A manufacturing licence for classical or patent/proprietary ASU drugs requires compliance with Schedule T.
review_note: Licence/GMP linkage checked in official2016 compilation pp179-181 and supplied2024 compilation. Schedule T covers manufacturing quality systems; current local implementation must be confirmed.

statute: New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019 (r.122E context)
title: New drug — proof of safety and efficacy required
text: A new/non-classical drug (including a novel Ayurveda-derived formulation making a new therapeutic claim) is regulated as a 'new drug' and must generate safety, efficacy and confirmatory clinical evidence before approval by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO). This is what separates a new drug (with genuine patent potential) from a classical medicine.
review_note: This note conflates the legacy Rule 122E/ Schedule Y framework with the 2019 rules and treats novel ASU claims too broadly. A current primary-source review is required.

section: G.S.R. 918(E), 30 Nov 2015 (r.2(eb); Rule 122-A/122E; Appendix IB of Schedule Y)
title: Definition and regulation of a phytopharmaceutical drug
text: G.S.R. 918(E) dated 30 November 2015 inserted the definition: a 'phytopharmaceutical drug' includes a purified and standardised fraction with a defined minimum of four (4) bio-active or phyto-chemical compounds (qualitatively and quantitatively assessed) of an extract of a medicinal plant or its part, for internal or external use in the diagnosis, treatment, mitigation or prevention of disease, excluding parenteral administration. It is regulated as a NEW DRUG by CDSCO under Rule 122E read with Appendix IB of Schedule Y, requiring identity, safety and confirmatory clinical data.

statute: Food Safety and Standards (Ayurveda Aahara) Regulations, 2022
title: Ayurveda Aahar — food category definition
text: The FSS (Ayurveda Aahara) Regulations, 2022 define 'Ayurveda Aahara' as a food prepared in accordance with the recipes, ingredients or processes as per the method described in the authoritative books of Ayurveda listed under Schedule A of these regulations, including products with other botanical ingredients consistent with the concept of Ayurveda Aahara, but does NOT include Ayurvedic drugs or proprietary Ayurvedic medicines, cosmetics, narcotic or psychotropic substances. Such products are licensed as food by FSSAI, not as drugs, and advertising must avoid disease claims.

statute: The Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954
title: Prohibition of objectionable advertisements
text: The DMR Act prohibits advertisements that claim to diagnose, cure or prevent the diseases/conditions listed in its Schedule, and prohibits misleading advertisements of drugs (including ASU medicines). It is the principal control on disease-claim advertising for Ayurvedic products and was central to the Patanjali/IMA misleading-advertisements litigation.

statute: The Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 — Rule 170 (omission saga)
title: Rule 170: dated timeline of omission and Supreme Court orders
text: Rule 170 required prior approval of advertisements of Ayurvedic/Siddha/Unani drugs by the State Licensing Authority. Timeline: the AYUSH Ministry directed non-enforcement (Aug 2023); Rule 170 was OMITTED by the Drugs (Fourth Amendment) Rules 2024 (G.S.R. 360(E), effective 01 Jul 2024); the Supreme Court STAYED that omission on 27 Aug 2024 during the IMA/Patanjali contempt case; and on 11 Aug 2025 the Supreme Court VACATED that stay and disposed of the IMA petition. The dossier reports that the omission consequently stood after that order, while ASU advertising remained subject to the DMR Act 1954. This is a dated research timeline, not confirmation of the rule's present legal status; later orders and notifications must be checked.
review_note: Dated research record; current status and counts have not been checked live.

statute: Biological Diversity Act, 2002, as amended by Act 10 of 2023
section: s.6(1), s.6(1A), s.6(1B); Amendment Act s.8, pp.3-4
title: Biodiversity IP duties: approval, registration and commercialisation depend on applicant category
text: For IP based on research or information on a biological resource accessed from India (including resources deposited in repositories outside India), or associated traditional knowledge, the 2023 amendment distinguishes applicant categories. Under s.6(1), persons or entities covered by s.3(2) require NBA approval before grant of the intellectual property right. Under s.6(1A), persons covered by s.7 require NBA registration before grant. Under s.6(1B), such s.7 persons who obtain the IP right require prior NBA approval at the time of commercialisation. These are not a single, uniform approval-before-filing rule for every applicant. Establish the applicant category and check current NBA procedures before acting.
review_note: Checked against the consolidated Indian statutory text hosted by WIPO Lex, archived as corpus/primary/bda-consolidated.pdf, and the official 2023 amendment. The amendment commenced on 1 April 2024 under S.O. 295(E), 18 January 2024. Related procedures are separately covered by bda_ipr_forms, bda_origin_2025 and bda_abs_2025.

statute: Biological Diversity Act, 2002, as amended by Act 10 of 2023
section: s.7(1) proviso, s.7(2)-(3); Amendment Act s.9, p.4
title: SBB intimation exemptions and the cultivated-plant certificate requirement
text: Section 7(1) requires persons outside s.3(2) to give prior intimation to the concerned State Biodiversity Board before accessing biological resources and associated knowledge for commercial utilisation, subject to the Act. Its proviso lists codified traditional knowledge, cultivated medicinal plants and their products, local people and communities including growers and cultivators, and vaids, hakims and registered AYUSH practitioners practising indigenous medicine as a profession for sustenance and livelihood. Under s.7(2), the cultivated medicinal plant exemption is available only if a certificate of origin is obtained from the Biodiversity Management Committee in the prescribed manner; s.7(3) addresses its issue from maintained records. This section-specific exemption should not be presented as a blanket waiver of all IP-related or benefit-sharing obligations; check the applicable applicant, material, sourcing and regulatory conditions.
review_note: Checked against the consolidated Indian statutory text hosted by WIPO Lex, archived as corpus/primary/bda-consolidated.pdf, and the official 2023 amendment. The amendment commenced on 1 April 2024 under S.O. 295(E), 18 January 2024. Related procedures are separately covered by bda_ipr_forms, bda_origin_2025 and bda_abs_2025.

statute: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
title: Geographical Indications for region-linked Ayurvedic goods
text: Section2(1)(e) defines a GI by geographical origin to which a given quality, reputation or other characteristic is essentially attributable; for manufactured goods at least production, processing or preparation must occur there. Section11 permits a producer-representative association/organisation/authority to apply; s17 permits qualifying producers to register as authorised users of an existing GI. Section21 protects use of the indication for the registered goods. A private novel formula does not itself establish a GI claim: a qualifying region-linked good and producer entitlement must be shown. The GI Registrar/Registry handles this route; a GI does not create ownership of every medicinal plant or technique from India.
review_note: Checked Indian statutory text via WIPO Lex, archived gi-act.pdf. Current GI register and specification for any particular herb or product were not searched.

title: Brand protection for Ayurvedic products
text: A trade mark under s.2(1)(zb) is capable of graphical representation and of distinguishing one person's goods/services, potentially including names, logos, packaging, shapes and colour combinations. Sections9 and11 impose distinctiveness, descriptiveness, deception and earlier-mark/confusion restrictions. Section18 governs applications to the Registrar; ss3-5 establish the Registrar/Trade Marks Registry. Registration under s.28 protects use of the mark for registered goods/services, subject to limits, and s.25 provides renewable ten-year terms. This protects product branding, not exclusive rights in a chemical formulation, therapeutic effect, extraction technique or manufacturing process. Clearance and selection of a distinctive brand are practical steps; registration is not assured.
review_note: Checked cited provisions in Indian statutory text archived from WIPO Lex as trademarks-act.pdf. Packaging may qualify only as a distinguishing mark; s9(3) excludes specified functional/natural/substantial-value shapes.

title: Protection of the visual design of a product / packaging
text: The Designs Act protects the features of shape, configuration, pattern or ornament applied to an article that appeal to and are judged by the eye — e.g. a distinctive bottle, pack or applicator for an Ayurvedic product. Protection lasts 10 years, extendable by 5. The design must be new and original.

title: Copyright in labels, literature and databases
text: Section13 protects eligible original literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works, films and sound recordings, subject to the Act; s14 defines the corresponding exclusive acts. Original label artwork, written instructions and manuals may therefore be protected as works. Section17 governs first ownership, including stated employment/commission exceptions; assignments are addressed in ss18-19. Sections44-45 provide the Register and application route and s48 makes register entries prima facie evidence. This is protection for eligible expression, not a patent on the underlying formula or method. Company ownership of commissioned material should be established rather than assumed.
review_note: Checked statutory text via WIPO Lex, archived copyright-act.pdf; see separate copyright_scope for Copyright Office explanation of expression/ideas and automatic protection.

statute: The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001
title: Plant variety protection and farmers' rights
text: The PPV&FR Act offers registration for eligible plant varieties, with s14 application categories, s15 novelty/distinctiveness/uniformity/stability criteria for new varieties and the specified extant-variety criteria, and s16 applicant entitlement. Sections28-29 govern rights and exclusions, including the notified-genera/species framework. Section39 recognises farmers' breeding/registration and seed-related rights, subject to its branded-seed exception. This may be relevant if a company actually develops or is entitled to a registrable medicinal-plant variety; buying ordinary Ashwagandha or formulating several herbs does not itself create a variety right. Confirm the relevant species notification, eligible variety category and applicant entitlement with the PPV&FR Authority.
review_note: Checked statutory text amended through2021 via WIPO Lex, archived ppvfr-act.pdf, ss14-16,28-29,39. No claim that Ashwagandha or any of the unnamed plants is presently notified/registrable or free of another breeder's rights.

statute: Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (CSIR–Ministry of AYUSH)
title: TKDL — defensive publication, patent-office access only
text: The TKDL is a defensive database that documents codified Indian traditional knowledge (Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa, Yoga) as searchable prior art to pre-empt wrongful patents abroad. The dossier's dated snapshot of the official TKDL page records more than 4.54 lakh transcribed formulations/practices and has helped set aside/withdraw/amend more than 324 patent applications. Access to the FULL database is available to Patent Offices ONLY under a TKDL Access (Non-Disclosure) Agreement (16 offices per the official page); there is no public sign-up and no public API. IP-SAKTI does not ingest the restricted TKDL database; it uses a curated legal-reference corpus and public referral links. These access statements and counts should be rechecked with TKDL before use.
review_note: Dated research record; current status and counts have not been checked live.

title: Turmeric patent cancelled on CSIR challenge
text: US Patent 5,401,504 ('Use of turmeric in wound healing', assigned to the University of Mississippi Medical Center, granted 1995) was challenged by India's CSIR on the ground that turmeric's wound-healing use was long-known Indian traditional knowledge. On re-examination all claims were cancelled; the re-examination certificate issued in 1998. A landmark example of TK prior-art defeating a wrongful patent — the case that helped motivate the TKDL.

title: Neem patent revoked by the EPO (final 2005)
text: A European Patent Office patent (held by the US Department of Agriculture and W. R. Grace) relating to a neem-derived product was opposed on the basis that neem's relevant properties were long-known Indian traditional knowledge. The Opposition Division revoked the patent (2000) and the revocation became final on 8 March 2005 when the appeal was dismissed. A key biopiracy precedent alongside turmeric and basmati.
review_note: The supplied citation is a Wikipedia page, not the EPO opposition or appeal decision. Replace it with the primary decision before using this note as authority.

title: RiceTec basmati patent — 15 of 20 claims cancelled
text: RiceTec Inc. was granted US Patent 5,663,484 ('Basmati rice lines and grains') on 2 September 1997. After India (APEDA/CSIR) challenged it, the USPTO re-examination certificate (issued 29 January 2002) CANCELLED claims 1-7, 10 and 14-20 — i.e. 15 of the 20 original claims, including the broad basmati claims — confirming only claims 8, 9 and 11 and amending 12 and 13. RiceTec could not maintain a generic monopoly on 'basmati'. A leading GI/biopiracy precedent.

title: Patentable subject matter — plants, animals, sui generis PVP
text: TRIPS Article 27.3(b) allows WTO members to exclude from patentability plants and animals (other than micro-organisms) and essentially biological processes for their production, but requires protection of plant varieties either by patents or by an effective sui generis system, or a combination. India implements this via s.3(j) of the Patents Act and the PPV&FR Act, 2001. The provision is the international basis for India's plant/TK patent exclusions.

statute: Convention on Biological Diversity + Nagoya Protocol
section: CBD Art 15; Nagoya Protocol on ABS
title: Sovereignty over genetic resources and access-and-benefit-sharing
text: The CBD affirms states' sovereign rights over their biological resources and requires access on mutually agreed terms with prior informed consent. The Nagoya Protocol (2010, in force 2014) operationalises access and benefit-sharing (ABS) for genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge. India implements these through the Biological Diversity Act and the NBA/SBB structure — the international backbone of the ABS duties on Ayurvedic bio-resource use.

statute: WIPO Treaty on IP, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge (GRATK)
title: GRATK Treaty: adoption and entry-into-force conditions
text: The WIPO GRATK Treaty was adopted by consensus in Geneva on 24 May 2024. It establishes a mandatory patent DISCLOSURE requirement: where an invention is based on genetic resources, applicants must disclose the country of origin/source, and where based on associated traditional knowledge, the indigenous people or local community that provided it. Under Article 17 it enters into force three months after 15 eligible parties deposit instruments of ratification/accession. This record does not establish today's ratification count or entry-into-force status. Consult WIPO's live treaty-status record before treating the disclosure requirement as operative.
review_note: Dated research record; current status and counts have not been checked live.

title: International patent filing route
text: The PCT lets an applicant seek patent protection in many countries through a single international application, deferring national-phase costs and decisions (typically up to 30/31 months from priority). It does not grant a global patent; grant remains with each national/regional office. The route an Ayurveda-derived new drug or phytopharmaceutical would use to preserve international patent options.

title: International trade mark registration
text: The Madrid System allows registration and management of a trade mark in many member countries through one international application filed via the home office. The route to protect an Ayurvedic brand in export markets.

title: International design registration
text: The Hague System allows registration of up to 100 industrial designs in multiple member countries through a single international application. The route to protect the packaging/product design of an Ayurvedic product internationally.

title: Deposit of micro-organisms for patent purposes
text: The Budapest Treaty lets a patent applicant satisfy the disclosure requirement for an invention involving a micro-organism by a single deposit at any International Depositary Authority (IDA), recognised by all member states. Relevant where an Ayurveda-related invention involves a micro-organism (which, unlike plants, is patentable under s.3(j)).

statute: EU Directive 2004/24/EC (Traditional Herbal Medicinal Products Directive) + COM(2008)584
title: EU traditional-use herbal registration and the Ayurveda market-access barrier
text: Directive 2004/24/EC created a SIMPLIFIED traditional-use registration for herbal medicinal products in the EU, requiring evidence of at least 30 years of medicinal use, including at least 15 years within the EU, without new safety/efficacy clinical trials. The 2008 Commission report COM(2008)584 declined to extend the scheme to regulate whole traditional medical SYSTEMS as such (Ayurveda/TCM), calling that 'not appropriate for a global regulation of such medical practices' — but noted individual products can still qualify. The real product-level barrier for Ayurvedic products is the 15-years-in-EU use requirement, which the report acknowledges can prevent EU market access for third-country products.

statute: Magesh et al., 'Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools'
section: Stanford RegLab/HAI; arXiv:2405.20362; J. Empirical Legal Studies (2025)
title: Why citation-grounding and abstention matter
text: The Stanford RegLab/HAI study found that leading proprietary legal-AI research tools hallucinate materially despite RAG and 'hallucination-free' marketing: the arXiv abstract reports the tools each hallucinate between 17% and 33% of the time; the Stanford HAI write-up reports Lexis+ AI and Ask Practical Law AI producing incorrect information more than 17% of the time and Westlaw AI-Assisted Research more than 34%. This is the evidence base for IP-SAKTI's citation-verification and safe-abstention design, and for not relying on a general LLM.

title: Natural discoveries are not inventions
text: Section 3(c) excludes the mere discovery of a scientific principle or formulation of an abstract theory, or discovery of any living thing or non-living substance occurring in nature. Discovering that a plant naturally contains a useful substance is not by itself a patentable invention; a proposed technical product or process must separately satisfy the Act.
review_note: Checked against the Indian statutory text hosted by WIPO Lex, archived as corpus/primary/patents-act.pdf. This verifies the cited provisions, not an exhaustive search for later amendments or case law.

title: Patent eligibility for technical products and processes
text: Section 2(1)(j) defines invention as a new product or process involving an inventive step and capable of industrial application. Section 2(1)(ja) requires technical advance over existing knowledge or economic significance or both, and non-obviousness to a skilled person. Section 2(1)(l) addresses anticipation by documents or use in India or elsewhere before filing with a complete specification. A formulation or extraction/manufacturing process may be a candidate, but being developed in-house or absent from classical Ayurvedic texts does not establish these conditions or avoid section 3 exclusions.
review_note: Checked against the Indian statutory text hosted by WIPO Lex, archived as corpus/primary/patents-act.pdf. This verifies the cited provisions, not an exhaustive search for later amendments or case law.

title: Patent disclosure and biological source/origin
text: A complete specification must fully and particularly describe the invention and its operation or use and method of performance, disclose the best method known to the applicant for which protection is claimed, and define the scope through claims. The biological-material provision requires disclosure of source and geographical origin when used in an invention. Failure to disclose, or wrong disclosure of, source or geographical origin is a ground of opposition under s.25(1)(j) and revocation under s.64(1)(p). Required enabling details and the best method cannot simply be withheld from a patent specification as trade secrets.
review_note: Checked against the Indian statutory text hosted by WIPO Lex, archived as corpus/primary/patents-act.pdf. This verifies the cited provisions, not an exhaustive search for later amendments or case law.

title: Preserving novelty before filing and patent publication
text: Worldwide publication and use matter to novelty under s.2(1)(l). Section 11A provides for publication of patent applications, subject to specified exceptions; sections 29-34 contain limited anticipation exceptions. Section 9(1) gives twelve months to file a complete specification after a provisional specification. A practical inference is to control public disclosure of the formula, proportions, extraction parameters, dose-related technical data and process before deciding what to file. There is no general safe assumption that every voluntary pre-filing disclosure is protected by a grace period.
review_note: Checked against the Indian statutory text hosted by WIPO Lex, archived as corpus/primary/patents-act.pdf. This verifies the cited provisions, not an exhaustive search for later amendments or case law.

title: Patent rights and the Indian Patent Office
text: Section 48 gives a patentee, subject to the Act, rights to prevent specified unauthorised acts concerning a patented product or patented process and products directly obtained by that process in India. Sections 73-74 identify the Controller of Patents and Patent Office. Patent rights do not by themselves establish that sale is lawful under drug regulation or that the product avoids another person's patent; separate regulatory and freedom-to-operate assessments follow from these distinct legal questions.
review_note: Checked against the Indian statutory text hosted by WIPO Lex, archived as corpus/primary/patents-act.pdf. This verifies the cited provisions, not an exhaustive search for later amendments or case law.

statute: The Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Drugs Rules, 1945
title: State licensing is required for ASU manufacture for sale
text: Section 33EEC(c) prohibits manufacture for sale or distribution of ASU drugs except under and in accordance with a licence issued by the prescribed authority, subject to the section's exceptions. Rule 152 provides for State-appointed licensing authorities; rules 153-154 govern the manufacturing application and licence (Form 24D and Form 25D). Rule 157 specifies licence conditions. An ordinary company commercial launch should establish the competent State/UT ASU licensing authority, manufacturing premises and applicable licence conditions. A proprietary ASU category does not automatically become a CDSCO new drug merely because its formula is novel.
review_note: Act s.33EEC and rules152-154,157 checked in official2016 compilation; the same core authority/form provisions were cross-checked in supplied CDSCO Drugs Rules compilation amended1July2024 pp168-175. Fees, filing workflow and later notifications need confirmation.

statute: The Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Drugs Rules, 1945
title: Mandatory ingredient disclosure limits formulation secrecy
text: Section 33EEC(a)(ii) requires the true list of ingredients on a proprietary ASU medicine label/container in the prescribed manner. Rule 161(1) specifically requires the true list of ingredients of patent/proprietary ASU drugs, botanical names of plant ingredients, their parts and forms, and quantities. A long list may be printed separately and enclosed with a label reference. Consequently, a trade-secret strategy cannot depend on concealing these mandatory ingredient/quantity disclosures after commercial sale. Undisclosed process know-how needs a separate confidentiality assessment.
review_note: Checked official2016 compilation pp28,190 and supplied2024 compilation pp190-191; do not confuse lawful pre-filing confidentiality with a right to omit mandatory labelling information.

title: Manufacturing and raw-material records
text: Rule 157A requires licensed ASU manufacturers to record raw materials used in the preceding financial year in Schedule TA and submit the record to the State Drug Licensing Authority and National Medicinal Plants Board or its nominated agency by 30 June of the succeeding financial year. Rule 158(a) requires manufacturing and test records for raw materials and finished products; rule 160 requires identification and available genuineness tests and their records. These records are distinct from biodiversity origin certificates and ABS agreements.
review_note: Checked in official2016 compilation pp181,185 and cross-checked in supplied2024 compilation. Confirm current reporting portal and any later amendments before submission.

statute: WIPO overview of the Indian trade-secret system (June 2024)
section: Sections 1-3 and 5 of the WIPO India country overview; Contract Act s.73 and Specific Relief Act s.38 discussed
title: Confidential know-how and limits of trade-secret protection
text: The WIPO India overview (June 2024) reports protection of confidential formulae and technical know-how through contracts (including NDAs and employment confidentiality clauses) and common-law breach of confidence. The information itself must be confidential; publicly known processes do not qualify merely because a contract labels them secret. Protection depends on the facts and obligations of confidence and generally does not prevent reverse engineering through a confidentiality clause. This is an official intergovernmental overview, not an enacted Indian trade-secret statute; it reports no separate exclusive trade-secret statute at that date. A practical strategy is access controls and documented confidentiality obligations for genuinely secret process know-how, assessed alongside patent disclosure and mandatory drug labels. Current law and enforceability of particular restrictions need professional confirmation.
review_note: Read archived WIPO country overview pp1-2; the source dates itself June2024. Its contractual/common-law summary is not a binding judgment or proof of the current absence of legislation. Criminal-law and restrictive-covenant details were deliberately not used.

statute: Biological Diversity Act, 2002, as amended in 2023
title: Biodiversity scope depends on material, activity and actual source
text: Access includes collecting, procuring or possessing biological resources occurring in or obtained from India or associated traditional knowledge for research, bio-survey or commercial use. Biological resources include plants, genetic material and derivatives, excluding value-added products; s.2(p) defines value-added products by unrecognisable and physically inseparable plant/animal portions or extracts. Commercial utilisation expressly includes drugs and extracts. Codified traditional knowledge is knowledge derived from First Schedule authoritative books. A medicinal product label, Indian plant species name, purchase from a trader, or final-product processing alone does not establish the access history or all exemptions; assess the actual material and sourcing chain.
review_note: Checked against the consolidated Indian statutory text hosted by WIPO Lex, archived as corpus/primary/bda-consolidated.pdf, and the official 2023 amendment. The amendment commenced on 1 April 2024 under S.O. 295(E), 18 January 2024.

statute: Biological Diversity Act, 2002, as amended in 2023
section: ss.3(1)-(2); amendment s.5; Biological Diversity Rules, 2024 r.13
title: Section 3 applicant status and prior NBA access approval
text: Section 3 requires previous NBA approval for obtaining covered biological resources occurring in India or associated knowledge for research, commercial utilisation or bio-survey/bio-utilisation by persons in s.3(2). Those categories are non-citizens; Indian citizens who are non-residents under Income-tax Act s.2(30); entities not incorporated/registered in India; and Indian-incorporated/registered entities controlled by a foreigner within Companies Act s.2(27). The 2023 amendment replaced the older foreign participation test with foreign control. Indian incorporation by itself does not settle the category. Rule13 uses Form1 for research/bio-survey and Form2 for commercial utilisation. Company control, citizenship/residence, purpose and actual access must be established.
review_note: Checked against the consolidated Indian statutory text hosted by WIPO Lex, archived as corpus/primary/bda-consolidated.pdf, and the official 2023 amendment. The amendment commenced on 1 April 2024 under S.O. 295(E), 18 January 2024. Rule13 independently checked in archived bda-rules-2024.pdf pp53-54.

statute: Biological Diversity Act, 2002, as amended in 2023
title: NBA, SBB and BMC roles and benefit-sharing duties
text: NBA regulates activities under sections3,4 and6 and determines benefit sharing when granting approvals. Section21(1) requires fair and equitable sharing of benefits from accessed biological resources, derivatives, innovations and related knowledge through mutually agreed terms between the applicant and the BMC represented by NBA. Section6(2) permits benefit-sharing fees, royalties or other financial-sharing conditions with IP approval. State Biodiversity Boards regulate s.7 activities under s.23(b); BMCs maintain cultivation records and issue origin certificates under s.7(2)-(3). These are distinct from patent grants and drug licences. Applicant/material-specific exemptions and regulations must be checked before determining liability.
review_note: Checked against the consolidated Indian statutory text hosted by WIPO Lex, archived as corpus/primary/bda-consolidated.pdf, and the official 2023 amendment. The amendment commenced on 1 April 2024 under S.O. 295(E), 18 January 2024.

statute: Biological Diversity (Access to Biological Resources and Knowledge Associated thereto and Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits) Regulations, 2025
title: 2025 ABS framework: separate access and IP-commercialisation routes
text: The 2025 Regulations supersede the2014 regulations, saving things previously done or omitted. Regulations4(1) and5(7) set commercial-access benefit-sharing tables by annual turnover: up to Rs5crore nil; above5 to50crore 0.2%; above50 to250crore 0.4%; above250crore 0.6% of annual gross ex-factory sale price of the product excluding Government taxes. Special provisions apply to high-value/conservation/threatened resources, and regs4(2)/5(9) require annual FormA statements for turnover above Rs1crore. Regulations8 and9 address IP commercialisation for s.3 and s.7 persons respectively: case-specific own-use benefit sharing up to1%, and licensing/assignment sharing up to5% of fees and up to5% of annual royalties, with the stated traditional-knowledge uplift and other conditions. Their explanations provide that during IP existence, covered access benefits are shared only under the relevant IP-commercialisation regulation. Reg11 supplies case-specific determination factors. Reg5 exemptions depend on their statutory/notification conditions, including notified mixed cultivated/non-cultivated products; they cannot be presumed for every herbal medicine. These are potential frameworks, not a calculation of the user's liability.
review_note: Read official NBA PDF English pp16-21. Notification dated29April2025; commencement is publication under reg1(2). No claim that every later notification, state process or fact-specific rate has been checked.

title: Biodiversity sourcing evidence and associated knowledge
text: FormB for s.7 prior intimation asks for applicant details and annual turnover; state-wise biological-resource common and scientific names, plant parts, quantities, access dates, source type (wild/cultivated/institution/repository/trader/market), geographical location, and trader/institution contacts or repository passport/origin data. It also asks whether associated knowledge is oral/documented and identifies the knowledge holder and address. Reg13 sets agreement content including resource details, intended uses, IP conditions and benefit sharing. A practical sourcing dossier should preserve invoices/batch links, the applicable approvals/agreements, origin certificates and provider records needed to substantiate these declared facts; not every such supporting document is a universally named statutory certificate.
review_note: Read official ABS2025 FormB pp23-24 and regs11-13 pp20-21. Invoice/batch links are a practical evidence recommendation, distinguished from expressly listed FormB fields.

section: G.S.R.295(E), 6 May 2025; substituted r.19; Forms11,11A,12; effective1 November2025
title: Cultivated medicinal-plant certificate procedure after November 2025
text: The 2025 amendment replaces r.19 from1November2025. BMCs maintain cultivated medicinal-plant records in Form11 on the web portal. Applications for a certificate of origin under s.7(2) are made to the BMC with the prescribed fee in Form11A on the portal; the certificate is generated as Form12 from those records. Form11 includes plant names, botanical/common names, cultivation period and approximate annual quantity; Form11A identifies applicant, State, district, BMC, plant and quantity. Form12 certifies cultivation within the BMC jurisdiction for the stated plant quantity. A supplier's generic cultivated assertion is not itself this certificate. Do not apply the superseded2024 r.19 procedure as the current one without checking the2025 substitution.
review_note: Checked official amendment English pp3-5. Effective date is1November2025. The portal and relevant BMC's operational implementation require confirmation.

title: NBA IP and foreign-source declarations under the 2024 rules
text: Rule16 provides Form7 for s.3(2) persons seeking NBA approval before IP grant; Form8 registration before grant for s.7 persons; and Form9 prior approval for commercialisation by s.7 persons. Rule18 requires a Form10 declaration from persons intending to use in India biological resources or associated traditional knowledge obtained from a foreign country for research, commerce or obtaining IP, under s.36A. Thus genuinely foreign sourcing has its own provider-country/Indian declaration analysis and is not proof that biodiversity compliance disappears. An NBA memorandum dated10July2025 reiterates Forms7/8/9/10 and requires the IP-form applicant name to exactly match the IP Office applicant name.
review_note: Checked Rules2024 pp55-57 and archived NBA memorandum bda-ipr-notice.pdf pp1-2 (10July2025). The memo is separately available at https://www.nbaindia.nic.in/sites/default/files/2026-07/imp_formIII.pdf. Confirm current portal instructions.

statute: Biological Diversity Act, 2002, as amended in 2023
title: Plant-variety rights have a section 6 exception
text: Section6(3) excludes applications for rights under laws protecting plant varieties from section6. Section6(4) requires the granting authority to endorse a copy of the grant document to NBA. This is a section6 IP exception; it does not state that all underlying access, material sourcing or other biodiversity obligations disappear.
review_note: Checked against the consolidated Indian statutory text hosted by WIPO Lex, archived as corpus/primary/bda-consolidated.pdf, and the official 2023 amendment. The amendment commenced on 1 April 2024 under S.O. 295(E), 18 January 2024.

statute: Copyright Office, Government of India: A Handbook of Copyright Law
section: Handbook: Copyright; Work; Registration of Copyright (pp3,9)
title: Copyright covers original expression, not formula ideas
text: The Government Copyright Office handbook explains that copyright protects expressions, not ideas, and does not ordinarily protect methods, factual information, titles, names or short phrases. Acquisition of copyright is automatic without registration formalities, although registration entries are prima facie evidence. Applying this guidance, original artwork or writing about a formulation may qualify; the formulation, manufacturing method and facts as such are not monopolised by copyright. This historical handbook is used only for these scope principles, not its outdated office details, fees or procedural forms.
review_note: Government Copyright Office handbook mirrored by WIPO Lex, archived copyright-handbook.pdf. The document has no clear publication date: as_of is retrieval date only, not a legal commencement/current-consolidation date. Only scope/automatic-protection passages on pp3,9 were used.

title: Inventor identification is separate from the right to apply for a patent
text: Subject to section 134, section 6 permits an application by a person claiming to be the true and first inventor, the assignee of that person in respect of the right to apply, or the specified legal representative of a deceased entitled person, alone or jointly. Section 7(2) requires proof of the right to apply when an application is made by virtue of an assignment of that right. Section 7(3) requires naming the person claiming to be the true and first inventor and the specified declaration when that person is not an applicant. Section 10(6) requires an inventorship declaration in the prescribed cases, form and period. The proviso to section 28(1) states that mention as inventor does not confer or derogate from rights under the patent. Applying these distinctions, identify the actual inventive contributors separately from the applicant or owner, and inspect the employment, research, university, contractor and assignment records rather than infer entitlement from payment or a job title. These passages do not establish the actual contribution or contractual title of any particular person.
review_note: Passages checked in the previously archived WIPO Lex statutory PDF, patents-act.pdf, PDF/printed pp.10-11,13,22-23. as_of follows the existing corpus provision date (1 January 2005), not a complete consolidation date; reviewed_on is passage review only. No employment dispute, university policy, later amendment or case-law survey was performed.

title: Written patent assignments and registration of patent title
text: Section 68 makes an assignment of a patent or share in a patent, mortgage, licence or creation of another patent interest invalid unless it is in writing and the agreement is reduced to a duly executed document embodying all terms and conditions governing the parties' rights and obligations. Section 69(1) requires a person acquiring the specified patent title or interest by assignment, transmission or operation of law to apply in writing in the prescribed manner to register the title or notice of interest. Section 69(2) also permits the specified other party to apply; section 69(3) concerns proof of title and permits the Controller to defer action on a dispute until a competent court determines rights. These are transactions concerning patent rights; proof of an assignment of the right to apply is separately addressed by section 7(2). Review the actual executed chain of title and retained rights rather than treat an NDA, payment, employment label or university affiliation as sufficient proof of ownership.
review_note: Checked patents-act.pdf, PDF/printed p.37, including section 68 and section 69(1)-(3). Section 68 amendment footnote identifies 1 January 2005. Review does not decide whether any pre-grant agreement transferred a particular invention, current procedural forms/deadlines, copyright ownership or the complete law as of 2026.

title: Cosmetic purpose and the Ayurveda drug-category boundary
text: Section 3(aaa) defines a cosmetic as an article intended to be rubbed, poured, sprinkled, sprayed on, introduced into or otherwise applied to the human body or any part for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness or altering appearance, including an article intended as a cosmetic component. Sections 3(a) and 3(b)(i) address the specified medicinal purposes, including diagnosis, treatment, mitigation or prevention of disease or disorder; the classical ASU definition additionally requires the stated authoritative-book formula condition. Applying these definitions, an Ayurveda-related hair or skin product intended only for cleansing or appearance may fit the cosmetic definition, while therapeutic intended use requires drug-category assessment. The presence of Ayurvedic ingredients or the word Ayurvedic alone does not determine classification. Review the complete formulation, intended function, presentation, labelling and advertising claims; these definitions do not certify a specific product or licensing exemption.
review_note: Checked official CDSCO compilation amended through 31 December 2016, archived dc-act-2016.pdf, PDF/printed pp.6-7, with headings and amendment footnotes. This is a dated definition check, not a 2026 consolidation, product approval, exemption finding or State classification decision. Cosmetic manufacturing procedure is a separate record based on the Cosmetics Rules, 2020.

title: Cosmetic manufacturing licence route in the 2020 Gazette
text: In the 15 December 2020 Gazette, rule 4(2) identifies the State Licensing Authority as the competent authority for cosmetics manufacture for sale or distribution. Rule 23(1)-(2) prescribes applications to that authority in COS-5 for a licence or COS-6 for a loan licence, with the specified fees and documents; it permits offline applications until the identified online portal operates. Rule 23(4) requires a COS-7 declaration of compliance with GMP, premises, plant and equipment requirements under the Seventh Schedule. Rule 25 specifies COS-8 for a manufacturing licence and COS-9 for a loan licence. Rule 3(p) describes a loan licence as use of another licensee's site for the cosmetic manufactured there. Rule 3(r) defines a new cosmetic by a novel ingredient not used anywhere in the world or not recognised for cosmetic use in national or international literature; rule 23(3) requires prior Central Licensing Authority permission in COS-3 for that category. This checked base Gazette supplies a route to assess, not proof of the complete law in 2026, satisfaction of licence conditions, current fees, operational portals or a product-specific exemption.
review_note: Downloaded from the official CDSCO Cosmetics Rules listing on 28 September 2026; archived cosmetics-rules-2020.pdf. Read Gazette PDF/printed pp.73-75,80-81, including rule 23 and the rule 3(r) new-cosmetic definition. as_of is the Gazette date, not 2026 legal currency. Later amendments, detailed schedules, State workflows and individual ingredient status have not been exhaustively checked.
